name: Opioid-Induced Constipation
preview_text: ใน TCM อาการท้องผูกที่เกิดจากฝิ่นไม่ใช่ภาวะเดียว แต่เป็นห้ารูปแบบที่แตกต่างกัน สิ่งสำคัญคือความรู้สึกของอุจจาระและสิ่งอื่นๆ ที่เกิดขึ้นในร่างกายของคุณ ผู้ป่วยส่วนใหญ่...

conventional_description: Opioid-induced constipation (OIC) is a very common side effect of opioid pain medications. Opioids bind to mu-receptors in the bowel, slowing the rhythmic contractions that move stool along, reducing fluid secretion, and increasing water absorption. The result is hard, dry stools, infrequent bowel movements, straining, and a sense of incomplete evacuation. Diagnosis is usually based on a person’s medication history and symptoms; there are no specific lab tests required. OIC often persists for as long as the opioid is taken and does not improve with time the way some other side effects might.
conventional_treatments:
Standard care usually begins with lifestyle measures - increasing fiber, fluid intake, and physical activity - though these are often insufficient on their own. Over-the-counter osmotic laxatives (like polyethylene glycol) and stimulant laxatives (like senna or bisacodyl) are commonly used.
When these fail, prescription medications may be added, including peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonists (PAMORAs) such as methylnaltrexone, naloxegol, or naldemedine, or the chloride channel activator lubiprostone. In some cases, enemas or manual disimpaction are necessary.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, opioids are seen as warm, acrid, and drying substances. When they enter the body, they tend to “use up” the cooling, moistening fluids (Yin) that keep the Large Intestine lubricated, and they can also disrupt the downward movement of Qi that propels stool through the bowel. The result is constipation, but the exact picture depends on your own underlying constitution and how long you have been taking the medication.
The Large Intestine is the organ most directly affected. When its Yin fluids are depleted, the stool becomes dry, hard, and pellet-like - a pattern called Large Intestine Dryness. When the bowel’s Qi flow gets stuck, you feel bloated, crampy, and strain even when the stool isn’t particularly dry - that’s Large Intestine Qi Stagnation. These two patterns are the most direct consequences of opioids’ drying and dispersing nature.
But the Spleen, Liver, and Kidneys are also involved. Opioids can weaken the Spleen’s ability to transform fluids, leading to a pattern of Spleen Deficiency with Dampness: sticky, difficult stools with fatigue and a heavy sensation. They can jam the smooth flow of Liver Qi, generating heat that further dries the bowels - Liver Qi Stagnation transforming into Heat. And over time, they can drain the Kidneys’ deepest Yin reserves, causing extreme dryness with night sweats and a red, peeled tongue - Kidney Yin Deficiency with Empty-Heat Blazing. This is why two people on the same opioid can have completely different constipation experiences, and why TCM tailors treatment to the individual pattern rather than just the symptom.
classical_quote: 「趺阳脉浮而涩，浮则胃气强，涩则小便数，浮涩相搏，大便则硬，其脾为约，麻子仁丸主之。」
classical_translation: "The pulse at the instep is floating and rough; floating indicates strong Stomach Qi, rough indicates frequent urination. When floating and rough contend, the stool becomes hard; the Spleen is constrained, and Ma Zi Ren Wan governs this."

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner starts by asking what the stool actually feels like and what other sensations come with it. Because opioids are warm and drying, they tend to deplete fluids or block the bowel’s downward movement, but the exact pattern depends on your underlying constitution and how long you have been taking the medication.
If the stools are extremely dry, hard, and difficult to pass, with thirst or a sensation of heat, the picture points to Large Intestine Dryness. The tongue may be red with a dry yellow coat, and the pulse fine and possibly choppy. This reflects a straightforward fluid deficit caused by the drug’s drying effect on the bowels.
When the main complaint is a feeling of incomplete evacuation, bloating, and straining even though the stool is not particularly dry, the focus shifts to Large Intestine Qi Stagnation. The abdomen may feel distended, and the tongue coat is often thin white or slightly yellow, with a wiry pulse. This indicates that the bowel’s propulsive force is stuck.
If the constipation alternates with loose stools, or the stool is sticky and difficult to wipe clean, accompanied by fatigue, poor appetite, and a heavy sensation, the Spleen Deficiency with Dampness pattern is likely. The tongue appears pale and swollen with a greasy coating, and the pulse is weak. Here the problem is both a lack of energy and an accumulation of dampness.
When constipation flares with emotional stress, and you feel irritable, bloated, and have a bitter taste or dry mouth, the Liver Qi Stagnation transforming into Heat pattern is at play. The tongue may be red with a yellow coat, and the pulse wiry and rapid. Stagnant Qi generates heat, which further dries the bowels and aggravates the blockage.
In chronic cases, especially with night sweats, hot palms and soles, and very dry, pellet-like stools, the root is Kidney Yin Deficiency with Empty-Heat. The tongue is red with little or no coating, and the pulse is thin and rapid. This deep fluid loss allows empty heat to scorch the intestines, making the stool extremely dry and hard.

patterns.better_with: Drinking warm water, Moistening foods (pears, honey), Gentle abdominal massage, Regular meal times, Gentle movement, walking, stretching, or light exercise
patterns.why_this_happens: Opioid medications have a warm, drying nature. They consume the body's Yin fluids, especially in the Large Intestine, leaving it parched and unable to lubricate the stool. This results in hard, dry stools that are difficult to pass.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Red, thin, dry body with cracks, thin dry slightly yellow coat. Pulse: Fine (thin), possibly choppy, weaker in the right Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Opioids are warming and drying, so anything that adds more heat or dryness-like spicy food, alcohol, or overwork-worsens fluid depletion. Moistening foods and warm water directly replenish the Yin fluids that the Large Intestine needs to lubricate stool. Gentle movement and massage help circulate Qi and fluids, easing the stagnation caused by the drug's acrid, dispersing nature.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Sip warm water throughout the day and eat moistening foods like pear, honey, sesame oil, and cooked apples. Avoid coffee, alcohol, and spicy or fried foods that further dry the body. Gentle walking or abdominal massage can help stimulate bowel movement.

patterns.pattern_name: Liver Qi Stagnation that transforms into Heat
patterns.symptoms: ["Irritability and explosive anger", "Bitter taste in the mouth", "Distending or burning pain along the ribs", "Dry mouth and throat", "Constipation with dry, hard stools", "Headache at the temples"]
patterns.worse_with: Emotional stress, anger, or frustration, Spicy, fried, or greasy foods, Alcohol and caffeine, Sedentary lifestyle or lack of exercise
patterns.better_with: Cooling, light meals, Deep breathing and meditation, Gentle movement, walking, stretching, or light exercise, Expressing emotions freely
patterns.why_this_happens: Opioids have an acrid, dispersing nature that can jam the smooth flow of Liver Qi, especially when emotional stress is present. Stuck Liver Qi generates heat, like friction creating a spark, and that heat dries up the fluids that should be moistening the bowels. The result is stubborn constipation with dry stools, often accompanied by the bloating, irritability, and bitter taste that signal Liver fire.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, redder at the sides, with a yellow coating. Pulse: wiry and rapid (xian shu).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress and anger are the classic triggers that knot Liver Qi, generating heat that dries the intestines. Calming the mind and moving the body gently unknots that Qi, allowing it to flow downward and push stool through. Cooling foods and bitter herbs clear heat and replenish fluids, while spicy, greasy, and stimulating substances add more heat and stagnation, making the constipation worse.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods, as well as alcohol and caffeine-they add fuel to the heat. Choose cooling, moistening foods like cucumber, celery, pear, and spinach. Gentle daily movement such as walking, yoga, or tai chi helps keep Liver Qi flowing smoothly. Make time to decompress: breathing exercises, journaling, or talking through frustrations can prevent Qi from stagnating into heat.

patterns.why_this_happens: Opioids are warm, drying drugs. Over time they can drain the body's deepest reserves of Yin-the cooling, moistening essence stored in the Kidneys. patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin, dry body with little or no coating, possible cracks. Pulse: fine (细 xì) and rapid (数 shuò), especially weak at the rear (Kidney) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Yin is easily damaged by overwork, late nights, and heating foods. Rest and cooling, moistening foods help preserve and restore Yin, while gentle movement promotes Qi flow without depleting fluids. Avoiding heat and stress prevents further Yin consumption and the flaring of empty heat that dries the bowels.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat moistening, cooling foods like pears, black sesame, honey, and congee. Avoid spicy, fried, or drying foods. Stay hydrated with warm water. Prioritize rest and early nights-Yin is rebuilt during sleep. Gentle exercise like walking or tai chi helps Qi flow without depleting fluids.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really help with constipation from pain medication?
faqs.answer: Yes, acupuncture is a well-studied supportive therapy for opioid-induced constipation. It works by stimulating specific points on the abdomen, legs, and arms to encourage the bowel’s natural peristaltic movement and to regulate the nervous system. Many patients find that regular acupuncture, especially when combined with Chinese herbs, can reduce their reliance on laxatives and make bowel movements more comfortable.

faqs.question: How long does it take for Chinese herbs to work for opioid constipation?
faqs.answer: That depends on your pattern. For straightforward dryness or Qi stagnation, herbs often soften the stool and ease bloating within the first week. For deeper deficiency patterns, it may take 2-4 weeks to feel a noticeable difference, with continued improvement over a couple of months. Herbs are not a one-time fix; they gently retrain the bowel over time.

faqs.question: Will I still need my laxatives while doing TCM?
faqs.answer: Many people are able to reduce or stop their laxatives as TCM treatment takes effect, but this should be done gradually and under guidance. Do not stop any prescribed medication abruptly. Your TCM practitioner and your prescribing doctor can work together to adjust your regimen safely as your bowel function improves.

faqs.question: Is it safe to take Chinese herbs with my pain medication?
faqs.answer: Chinese herbs are generally safe to combine with opioids, but it is essential that both your TCM practitioner and your medical doctor know exactly what you are taking. Some herbs, like rhubarb (Da Huang), have a laxative effect and could compound the action of other laxatives. Always bring a full list of your medications and supplements to your TCM consultation so the formula can be tailored safely.

faqs.question: What foods should I avoid if I have opioid-induced constipation?
faqs.answer: In TCM, the guiding principle is to avoid foods that are drying or difficult to digest. This includes spicy foods, fried foods, alcohol, and excessive coffee. For some patterns, raw and cold foods (like salads and iced drinks) can weaken the Spleen and make constipation worse. Instead, focus on warm, moistening foods like cooked pears, spinach, sesame seeds, and honey water.

faqs.question: Does TCM work for severe OIC that hasn’t responded to prescription laxatives?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM often helps even when conventional treatments have stalled because it addresses the underlying pattern, not just the symptom. In severe cases, a combination of acupuncture, a custom herbal formula, and dietary adjustments can gradually restore the bowel’s own rhythm. However, patience is key; severe, long-standing constipation may take several months of consistent treatment to turn around.

faqs.question: Can TCM prevent constipation when I first start taking opioids?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. Starting TCM early - ideally within the first week of opioid therapy - can help protect the Large Intestine’s fluids and keep Qi moving. This proactive approach may reduce the severity of constipation or prevent it from becoming entrenched. Many cancer centers now integrate acupuncture and herbal medicine from the beginning of opioid treatment for this reason.

research.title: Observation on the therapeutic effect of thumbtack needle therapy on refractory constipation induced by opioids
research.description: This clinical observation compared thumbtack needle therapy (a form of intradermal acupuncture) with standard care in patients suffering from refractory opioid-induced constipation. The acupuncture group showed significantly greater improvements in bowel movement frequency, stool consistency, and abdominal distension, with no serious adverse events reported.
research.periodical: Shanghai Journal of Acupuncture and Moxibustion, 2021, 40(9): 1085-1089.

research.title: Research progress on acupoint application therapy for opioid-induced constipation
research.description: This review article summarizes the clinical evidence for acupoint application (herbal paste applied to acupuncture points) in treating opioid-induced constipation. It reports that acupoint application can improve bowel function, reduce laxative dependence, and enhance quality of life, with a favorable safety profile.
research.periodical: Open Access Journal of Clinical Trials, 2023, 15: 23-30.

research.title: Analysis of medication rules of traditional Chinese medicine in the treatment of opioid-induced constipation based on the Traditional Chinese Medicine Inheritance Support Platform
research.description: This data-mining study analyzed 120 herbal prescriptions for opioid-induced constipation and identified core herb combinations. The most frequently used herbs were Huo Ma Ren, Da Huang, and Hou Po, reflecting the dominant treatment principles of moistening dryness, moving Qi, and draining heat.
research.periodical: Beijing Journal of Traditional Chinese Medicine, 2023, 42(9): 1023-1027.
